title: Chapter 100: Hensheng: To Hate Life 3
content:
Chapter 100

The silence that followed was absolute.

Nobody breathed. The courtyard froze in sheer, unadulterated shock.

Jin Guangyao’s fingers went slack, the chord slipping loose from his grip. The instant the stinging pressure on his throat vanished, Wei Wuxian lunged across the flagstones and threw himself violently into Lan Wangji’s arms.

That thunderous, shameless declaration had detonated like a lightning strike, leaving Lan Wangji completely paralyzed. His usually stoic, carved-marble features cracked, showing a rare, utterly bewildered daze. It was hardly the first time Wei Wuxian had wrapped both arms around his waist in a death-grip, but tonight, Lan Wangji felt like a solid block of wood—so stiff and frozen he didn't even know where to put his hands.

Wei Wuxian grabbed his collar, panting straight into his chest. "Lan Zhan, did you hear me?! Did you hear what I just said?!"

Lan Wangji’s lips parted, trembling slightly before he managed a strained murmur: "You..."

The man was famous for his razor-sharp brevity; he never stumbled, never hesitated, and never minced words. Yet right now, every syllable scraped out in disjointed shock.

"You said just now..."

He clearly wanted to repeat the words just to make sure his ears weren't playing cruel tricks on him, but a phrase like that was simply too scandalous for Hanguang-jun to force past his teeth.

Seeing him choke, Wei Wuxian didn't hesitate for a fraction of a second to supply the rerun: "I said I genuinely wanted to go to bed with—"

A sharp throat-clearing cut through the air.

Standing a few paces away, Lan Xichen pressed a curled fist against his mouth, coughing with immense, agonizing effort. After an excruciating pause, the sect leader let out a weary sigh. "Master Wei. Your timing... and your choice of venue... are truly something else."

Wei Wuxian offered an apology dripping with zero sincerity. "Really sorry about that, Lan-zongzhu, but I couldn't hold it in for another second."

Across the courtyard, it seemed Jin Guangyao couldn't wait another second either. Whirling around, he snapped, “Haven't you dug it up yet?!”

A monk called back, sweating profusely, "Sect Leader, you buried it far too deep back then..."

Jin Guangyao’s face cycled violently between green and pale, looking thoroughly sick. Still, he kept his temper on a tight leash, snapping, "Pick up the pace!"

A jagged crack of white lightning tore across the heavens, followed seconds later by a concussive roll of thunder. Jin Guangyao glanced skyward, his jaw tightening as an icy drizzle began to sweep over the rooftops.

Wei Wuxian clung to Lan Wangji, a torrential sea of confessions backed up behind his teeth, but the freezing rain misting across his cheeks forced a drop of cold reason back into his skull.

Jin Guangyao turned to Lan Xichen, bowing slightly. "Er-ge, it’s pouring. Let’s head inside to get out of the rain."

Even with Lan Xichen completely under his thumb, Jin Guangyao maintained flawless etiquette, refusing to treat him with anything less than spotless deference. It was impossible to throw a punch at a smiling face, especially when Lan Xichen had never had much of a temper to begin with.

Jin Guangyao led the way over the wooden threshold, and the rest filed into the main hall behind him.

Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji had already scoped the interior out earlier that afternoon. It was cavernous and grand, the vermilion pillars and gilded lacquer looking practically brand new, clearly maintained with obsessive, expensive care. Deeper in the back, behind the altar, the disguised cultivators and monks were frantically shoveling dirt out of a trench that was already waist-deep, yet whatever prize Jin Guangyao had stashed away remained buried out of reach.

Glancing up at the altar, Wei Wuxian froze.

The grand Guanyin statue loomed overhead, sculpted with breathtaking delicacy. Unlike traditional depictions of the Bodhisattva—which favored maternal, rounded compassion—this figure carried a sharp, refined, feminine elegance. But what made his breath hitch was the face: the features were eerily familiar.

It looked almost identical to Jin Guangyao.

A passing glance might have hidden it, but comparing the stone carving directly to the man standing a few yards away, the resemblance was unmistakable, an easy five- or six-part match.

Wei Wuxian couldn't help the dry thought: was Jin Guangyao really that hopelessly conceited? Sitting atop the entire cultivation world as Chief Cultivator wasn't enough, so he had to carve his own face onto a deity just to hoard the incense and prayers of thousands of mortals? Or was this some bizarre occult cultivation technique he’d never heard of?

"Sit," Lan Wangji’s low voice murmured right against his ear.

The whisper yanked Wei Wuxian straight back to reality. Lan Wangji had gathered four prayer cushions from around the hall, offering two to Lan Xichen and Jin Ling, leaving the remaining pair for himself and Wei Wuxian. For reasons entirely unstated, both Lan Xichen and Jin Ling had dragged their cushions as far across the tiles as physically possible, studiously pretending the opposite wall was the most fascinating thing in the world.

Jin Guangyao and his inner circle had already ducked behind the altar partition to supervise the excavation. Wei Wuxian tugged Lan Wangji down onto the cushions. Perhaps still reeling from the shock, Lan Wangji swayed slightly as he sank onto his knees, steadying himself with an awkward breath.

Wei Wuxian took a second to rein in his own galloping pulse, locking his eyes onto Lan Wangji’s face.

The man kept his lashes lowered, his expression completely shuttered. Wei Wuxian knew that a single blurted declaration wouldn't be enough to patch up years of misunderstandings—not after he’d spent weeks smiling, teasing, and casually torturing Lan Wangji with fake affection. It was only natural for the man to assume this was another reckless prank. The thought made Wei Wuxian’s ribs ache with guilt and tender longing; he needed to hit him with something so raw, so undeniable, that no room for doubt remained.

"Lan Zhan," he said, his voice tight. "Look at me."

Lan Wangji’s throat moved. "Mm."

Dragging in a ragged breath, Wei Wuxian murmured, "My memory really is terrible. There’s so much from the past that I’ve completely blanked on. Including the Nightless City—what happened during those three days, I don't remember a single scrap."

Lan Wangji’s golden eyes widened a fraction.

Wei Wuxian reached out, slamming his palms flat against Lan Wangji’s shoulders, gripping him tight. "But! Starting from right now, every single word you say to me, every single thing you do for me, I will remember it all! Every single bit of it, for the rest of my life!"

Lan Wangji offered no reply, completely motionless.

Wei Wuxian pressed forward, unblinking: "You're incredible. I like you."

Still, Lan Wangji remained silent.

"Or let me put it this way: I adore you. I love you. I want you. I can't live without you. Do whatever the hell you want with me."

Not a word broke from Lan Wangji's lips.

"I want to night-hunt with you for the rest of my days."

Silence hung heavy between them.

Raising three fingers, pointing straight at the heavens, the earth, and his own chest, Wei Wuxian swore, "And I want to sleep with you every single day! I swear to you this isn't some impulsive whim, and I’m not teasing you like I used to, and it's definitely not out of some twisted debt of gratitude! None of that bullshit! I just love you so damn much that all I want is to climb into bed with you. I don't want anyone else—it has to be you, it can only be you! You can do whatever you want to me, however you like it, and I'll love every second of it, as long as you're willing to—"

A violent gale tore through the high eaves, slamming through the open doors and snuffing out the ranks of red candles in an instant.

Outside, the gentle drizzle had unspooled into a raging, torrential storm, violently battering the swaying paper lanterns until their flames drowned.

The entire hall plunged into absolute, pitch-black darkness.

Wei Wuxian’s breath choked off.

In the pitch black, an iron pair of arms caught him, hauling him flush against a broad chest as a mouth came crashing down, sealing his lips in a desperate, bruising kiss.

Lan Wangji’s breath was ragged and feverishly hot, murmuring raw, broken words right into his ear, "Adore you..."

Wei Wuxian threw his arms around his neck. "Yes!"

Lan Wangji’s voice shook, "Love you... Want you..."

"Yes!" Wei Wuxian shouted back.

"Can't live without you... want no one else... it can only be you.."

He echoed every confession Wei Wuxian had just poured out, his voice and body trembling so violently it almost felt as if he were on the brink of tears.

With every line, the arms around Wei Wuxian’s waist tightened another fraction, squeezing until his ribs screamed in protest. Yet Wei Wuxian only dug his fingers deeper into the man’s back, returning the crushing embrace until he could barely breathe. He leaned into the pain, wishing he could hold him even closer.

Neither could see a thing.

Yet with their chests pressed flush against one another, their hearts had nowhere to hide. Wei Wuxian could feel it clear as day—the furious, frantic thudding inside Lan Wangji’s ribs, a heat so scorching it threatened to tear through his flesh, and a solitary, silent drop of moisture that vanished against his neck, leaving him to wonder if it was only a trick of the rain.

A sharp clatter of hurried footsteps echoed from the rear hall as Jin Guangyao returned with his men. Two monks fought against the howling wind to shove the heavy doors shut, throwing the thick wooden bolt into place with a hollow thud. Jin Guangyao whipped out a fire talisman, blew lightly across the paper, and touched the yellow flame to the wick of an altar candle, casting the drafty, isolated hall in a faint, flickering amber glow.

Suddenly, a crisp double knock rattled the front door.

Someone was outside.

Every cultivator in the temple snapped to attention, blades clearing their sheaths as the monks barred the doors with their bodies. Jin Guangyao tilted his head, voice smooth and untroubled: "Who is it?"

A muffled voice called through the wood: "Sect Leader, it’s me!"

Su She.

Jin Guangyao flicked his fingers in a signal, and the monks slid the bolt back. Su She slipped inside amidst a violent gust of wind and rain.

The draft nearly snuffed the fresh candle flame, flickering violently until the doors were slammed shut again. Soaked to the bone, his lips pale purple from the chill, Su She held a drawn sword in his right hand—while his left was dragging an unconscious body by the collar. He moved to chuck the luggage onto the floor, only to freeze dead in his tracks, staring directly at Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji still huddled together on their prayer cushions.

Having eaten immense dirt at the hands of these two barely an hour ago, Su She bristled, sword half-raised as his eyes darted toward Jin Guangyao. Seeing his master lounging around looking totally unbothered, he deduced the two had already been neutralized, and his sneer returned.

Jin Guangyao glanced down. "What happened?"

Su She grunted, "Ran into him on the road. Figured he might be useful leverage, so I brought him along."

Jin Guangyao stepped closer. "Did you injure him?"

"No. Passed out from fright." Su She dropped the body with a wet splat.

Jin Guangyao sighed, shaking his head. "Minshan, you really must be gentler. The man is far too delicate to be thrown around like sacks of grain."

"Understood, sir," Su She muttered, hastily scooping the man back up and laying him down with exaggerated care beside Lan Xichen.

Lan Xichen pushed the wet, matted hair from the man's forehead, revealing the terrified, slack face of Nie Huaisang. He’d clearly been snatched on his way back to Qinghe after catching his breath at Lotus Pier.

Lan Xichen looked up, frowning. "Why drag Huaisang into this?"

"An extra clan leader in hand buys us a little more insurance," Jin Guangyao replied effortlessly. "Rest easy, Er-ge. You know how I've treated Huaisang over the years; once the dust settles, I will see to it that you both walk away without a scratch."

Lan Xichen’s tone was dead flat. "Am I supposed to believe that?"

Jin Guangyao chuckled. "Believe it or not, it hardly matters. Er-ge doesn't have much of a choice right now, does he?"

Su She’s cold, contemptuous gaze drifted toward the pair on the cushions.

He let out a sharp scoff. "Hanguang-jun, Yiling Laozu... What a surprise to run into you two again so soon. And look at that—the tables have completely turned. How's the view from down there?"

Lan Wangji didn't deign him with a look. Meaningless posturing had never been worth his breath.

Wei Wuxian thought privately: you ran for your life like a dog on the Burial Mounds, and you’re running for your life right now. What turned, exactly?

Years of bitter resentment had festered in Su She’s chest; he didn't need an audience to start venting his venom. Looking Lan Wangji up and down, he sneered, "Even backed into a corner, you still put on that pathetic, stoic, unflappable act. Just how long do you think you can keep pretending to be above it all?"

Silence was his only answer.

Lan Xichen intervened, his tone cool and measured: "Sect Leader Su. During your years studying under the Gusu Lan banner, our house never mistreated you. Why must you harbor such personal vitriol toward Wangji?"

Su She spat, "Who’d dare hold a grudge against the peerlessly gifted Second Young Master Lan? I just can't stand that arrogant face of his, strutting around like he's the center of the universe."

Wei Wuxian had known for two lifetimes that malice rarely needed a logical reason, but this was still remarkably petty. "Did Hanguang-jun ever say he thought he was the center of the universe? If memory serves, isn't there a rule carved right into the Gusu Lan precepts that strictly forbids arrogance and conceit?"

Jin Ling blurted out from the side, "How the hell do you know what's in the Gusu Lan rules?!"

Wei Wuxian rubbed his chin casually. "Write them out enough times and they kind of stick, kid."

"Why the hell would you be copying their rules?!" Jin Ling snapped, about to add that he wasn't one of them, but caught the words in his throat, flushing red before clamping his mouth shut.

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Sect Leader Su, could it be that just because Hanguang-jun has had an icy, deadpan expression since childhood, you decided he was looking down on you? Because if that’s the case, he’s taking the blame for free. He makes that exact same face at literally everyone. Honestly, you should thank your lucky stars you didn't study at the Yunmeng Jiang Clan."

Su She narrowed his eyes. "Why is that?"

"Because you would've dropped dead of sheer rage within three days," Wei Wuxian replied brightly. "Back when I was a kid, I woke up every single morning genuinely, deeply convinced that I was a goddamned prodigy of the century. And I didn't just keep that brilliant thought to myself—I bragged about it to every living soul I crossed paths with."

A thick blue vein throbbed against Su She’s temple. "Shut up!"

He lunged forward to throw a concussive palm strike, but Lan Wangji’s arm caught Wei Wuxian by the waist, sweeping him smoothly into his chest, shielding him behind broad shoulders. Su She’s strike hitched in midair, caught in hesitation, just as Wei Wuxian poked his chin over Lan Wangji’s shoulder.

"I wouldn't if I were you, Sect Leader Su. Lianfang-zun still holds Zewu-jun in rather high regard; if you go scuffing up Hanguang-jun, how happy do you think your master’s going to be?"

Su She had only hesitated because of that exact political calculus, but hearing Wei Wuxian spell it out made the humiliation burn ten times hotter. Gnashing his teeth, he fell back on cheap taunts: "To think the legendary Yiling Laozu—the terror of the underworld—is actually terrified of dying!"

Wei Wuxian beamed back, utterly shameless. "Flattery will get you everywhere. Though, strictly speaking, I’m not afraid of death; I just really don't feel like dying right now."

Su She sneered, "Petty semantics. Is there a difference between being afraid to die and not wanting to die?"

Snuggled securely in Lan Wangji’s lap, Wei Wuxian said, "Of course there's a difference. For instance: me not wanting to get off Lan Zhan right now, versus me being terrified of getting off Lan Zhan—think those two are the same thing?"

He paused, tilting his head. "Actually, my bad. Take that back. Now that I think about it, they're pretty much identical."

Su She’s face turned an impressive shade of mottled green.

Wei Wuxian had only meant to troll the man for sport, but right then, a faint, breathy sound drifted down from above.

A laugh.

It was feather-light, barely catching the air, subtle enough to make anyone think they’d imagined it.

Wei Wuxian whipped his chin up—and saw it with absolute, crystalline clarity. Resting at the corner of Lan Wangji’s mouth was a soft, breathtaking curve that had yet to fade, blooming across his pale features like early morning sun washing over fresh winter snow.

Su She froze. Lan Xichen stared. Even Jin Ling sat slack-jawed.

It was an open secret across the realm that Hanguang-jun was carved from arctic permafrost—aloof, stern, and entirely devoid of worldly mirth. Practically no living soul had ever witnessed him smile, let alone catch the corners of his lips curling in quiet amusement. Seeing that divine warmth surface in a drafty, enemy-infested shrine was an absolute shock to the system.

Wei Wuxian’s eyes went completely round.

His throat hitched, his Adam’s apple bobbing as he swallowed hard. "Lan Zhan, you..."

Before he could pull a thought together, a sharp knock rattled the main doors once more.

Su She’s blade cleared its scabbard in an instant. "Who's there?!"

No answer came.

The heavy double doors detonated into kindling.

Riding the howling wind and rain, an explosive arc of brilliant purple lightning slammed dead-center into Su She’s sternum, hurling him backward through the air. He smashed into a massive red-lacquered pillar with a concussive crack, coughing up a mouthful of dark blood before sliding to the tiles. The two monks stationed near the entrance were blasted off their feet by the raw spiritual shockwave, groaning on the floor.

A figure clad in deep violet stepped over the shattered threshold.

Outside, the storm raged with apocalyptic fury, yet the intruder was barely dampened, only the hem of his dark robes stained a deeper shade of plum. His left hand gripped the bamboo handle of an oiled-paper umbrella, rain clattering against the taut canopy in an angry hiss, while violent, crackling arcs of purple light coiled around the silver ring on his right hand, hissing like a nest of vipers.

His face was blacker than the midnight thunder.
